name: Culture and information
question: How is AI changing what gets made, what people attend to and believe, cultural diversity, and creators' ability to earn?
synthesis: AI can increase content production without attracting a matching share of genuine attention or creator income. Studies here find better individual outputs alongside greater similarity, persuasion alongside successful correction, and useful detection alongside language-dependent errors. Most evidence comes from selected platforms and short tasks, so it does not establish AI's overall share of culture or its economy-wide effect on creators.

facets.label: Production and provenance
facets.description: Amounts and sources of human, AI-assisted and fully synthetic content, keeping uploads separate from catalog stocks.

facets.label: Discovery and consumption
facets.description: Exposure, clicks, listening and sharing, including ranking, fraud and the difference between intended and observed behavior.

facets.label: Beliefs, trust and persuasion
facets.description: Accuracy judgments, authorship beliefs, opinion change and persistence under different human-AI interactions.

facets.label: Creative quality and diversity
facets.description: Individual quality, between-output similarity, distribution tails and diversity of consumed culture.

facets.label: Creator work and earnings
facets.description: Job demand, compensation, realized income and distribution of rewards, without treating engagement as revenue.

facets.label: Attribution reliability
facets.description: Reliability and fairness of human judgments, detectors and provenance measures across languages, domains and model versions.

sources.title: Deezer: AI music has surpassed 50% of new music uploads for the first time
sources.authors: Jesper Wendel (Deezer)
sources.design: Recurring platform operational disclosures using Deezer's proprietary music detector and fraud systems.
sources.population: Tracks delivered to Deezer and streams on that platform.
sources.geography: International Deezer service; not the entire music market.
sources.duration: Series since January 2025; inspected July 21, 2026 release reports June 2026 uploads and separate 2025 fraud statistics.
sources.measure: Daily fully AI-generated deliveries; share of daily deliveries; share of streams; flagged fraudulent AI streams.
sources.finding: Deezer reports about 90,000 fully AI tracks per day on average in June 2026, exceeding half of daily deliveries at peak, but only 1-3% of all platform streams. Its separate 2025 claim is that up to 85% of streams of fully AI tracks were fraudulent.
sources.limitations: Company-reported detector and fraud classifications are not independently validated here. Peak delivery share is not average catalog share. Differently dated stream/fraud estimates cannot be multiplied into a verified genuine-listening estimate.
sources.locator: Release opening paragraphs and AI music FAQ
sources.sourceNote: Read official release and FAQ; no raw logs. Tagging start is inconsistent between body and notes (June 2026 versus June 2025), requiring clarification.
sources.selectionReason: Recurring operational series directly separates production from consumption, with explicit proprietary-measurement limits.
sources.headline: Large synthetic upload flows do not imply comparable listening shares
sources.searchOrigin: Existing imported Deezer lead -> official July 2026 release and November 2025 survey release.

sources.title: Deezer/Ipsos survey: 97% of people can't tell the difference between fully AI-generated and human made music - clear desire for transparency and fairness for artists
sources.authors: Deezer and Ipsos; release by Jesper Wendel
sources.design: Online quota survey with a three-song blind classification task and stated-preference questions.
sources.population: 9,000 adults aged 18-65; streaming-user questions use a 6,791-person subset.
sources.geography: US, Canada, Brazil, UK, France, Netherlands, Germany and Japan.
sources.duration: October 6-10, 2025 fieldwork; published November 12, 2025.
sources.measure: Correct identification of all three tracks; attitudes to labeling and filtering.
sources.finding: 97% failed to classify all three tracks correctly (two AI, one human). This is not a 97% error rate per judgment. 80% of all respondents favored labeling; 45% of streaming users said they would filter AI music.
sources.limitations: Three selected stimuli cannot establish general detection ability. Quota sample, commercial sponsorship and hypothetical preferences limit inference to actual listening or payment.
sources.locator: Survey results and methodology note
sources.sourceNote: Official commissioned-survey summary inspected; questionnaire, microdata and stimulus-selection procedure not independently checked.
sources.searchOrigin: Deezer series -> November 2025 Ipsos release.

sources.title: Google users are less likely to click on links when an AI summary appears in the results
sources.authors: Athena Chapekis and Anna Lieb
sources.design: Observational browser panel with search-query reconstruction; no randomized assignment of AI summaries.
sources.population: 900 US adults; 68,879 unique Google searches, of which 12,593 generated summaries when reconstructed.
sources.geography: United States.
sources.duration: Browsing March 1-31, 2025; queries rerun April 7-17; report July 22.
sources.measure: Search visits followed by traditional-result clicks, summary-source clicks or session ending.
sources.finding: Traditional-result clicks occurred in 8% of visits with an AI summary versus 15% without; a summary-source link was clicked in 1% of visits with summaries.
sources.limitations: Query types differ and summaries were reconstructed after the browsing period. Association is not a randomized effect on publisher traffic or revenue. Search-level comparison does not estimate individual change over time.
sources.locator: How we did this; click-through comparison and methodology
sources.sourceNote: Full research article and methods note inspected. Classified as a one-window search-level snapshot despite repeated browser logs, not an ongoing audience series or longitudinal effect estimate.
sources.selectionReason: Observed click behavior anchors attention independently of supply; reconstruction and confounding limits remain visible.
sources.headline: AI-summary searches had fewer outbound clicks in one US panel
sources.searchOrigin: Existing Pew import -> original July 22, 2025 article and methods.

sources.title: Generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces the collective diversity of novel content
sources.authors: Anil R. Doshi and Oliver P. Hauser
sources.publisher: Science Advances; author manuscript on arXiv
sources.design: Randomized short-story writing with no AI idea, one GPT-4 idea or up to five ideas; independent ratings and embedding comparisons.
sources.population: 293 writers and 600 evaluators in the inspected manuscript.
sources.geography: Online English-language task; recruitment geography not extracted.
sources.duration: Single writing and evaluation sessions; inspected manuscript v3 dated March 14, 2024.
sources.measure: Rated novelty, usefulness and enjoyment; self-ratings; similarity between stories.
sources.finding: AI ideas improved evaluated story quality, especially for less-creative baseline writers, but made stories more similar to one another. Self-ratings and high-baseline-creativity writers showed less or no benefit on some measures.
sources.limitations: Constrained eight-sentence task and restricted prompting do not represent sustained artistic practice. Ratings and embedding similarity are distinct from cultural value or income.
sources.locator: Manuscript main results, experimental design and discussion, PDF pages 1-11
sources.sourceNote: Read author manuscript main text; publisher access unavailable. Version-specific sample retained; supplement not fully inspected or reanalyzed.
sources.selectionReason: Randomization identifies task-level assistance effects while explicitly measuring individual quality and collective similarity separately.
sources.headline: Better-rated individual stories can still become more alike
sources.searchOrigin: Search for human-AI creativity diversity experiments -> publisher DOI -> arXiv author manuscript.

sources.title: AI model GPT-3 (dis)informs us better than humans
sources.authors: Giovanni Spitale, Nikola Biller-Andorno and Federico Germani
sources.design: Survey experiment comparing accurate and false human-written and GPT-3 tweets and perceived authorship.
sources.population: Online respondents evaluating selected tweets; sample denominator not extracted from abstract.
sources.geography: Not established in inspected abstract.
sources.duration: Short exposure task; v2 January 31, 2023; field dates not verified.
sources.measure: Truth judgments, comprehensibility and human-versus-AI classification.
sources.finding: The authors report more understandable synthetic accurate messages and more convincing synthetic false messages; participants struggled to identify authorship.
sources.limitations: Selected topics and an older model; immediate judgments are not persistent belief change, actual sharing or population influence.
sources.locator: arXiv abstract and submission history
sources.sourceNote: Author abstract inspected, not full methods or stimulus appendix. No numeric effect extracted.
sources.searchOrigin: Search human AI disinformation persuasion -> author arXiv record.

sources.title: Durably reducing conspiracy beliefs through dialogues with AI
sources.authors: Thomas H. Costello, Gordon Pennycook and David G. Rand
sources.design: Personalized GPT-4 Turbo dialogue experiment with subsequent participant follow-up.
sources.population: 2,190 conspiracy-believing participants reported in original abstract.
sources.geography: Recruitment geography not verified in inspected abstract.
sources.duration: Original study reports two-month follow-up; publication September 2024.
sources.measure: Strength of belief in a nominated conspiracy before and after dialogue and at follow-up.
sources.finding: The original abstract reports a durable belief reduction. A June 11, 2026 editorial expression of concern now accompanies the article; the effect should not be treated as a secure headline finding while that uncertainty remains.
sources.limitations: Editorial concern materially qualifies reliability. No raw-data or correction audit was performed; an expression of concern is not itself a retraction.
sources.locator: Original abstract and linked Expression of Concern
sources.sourceNote: Checked PubMed original and notice https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42275523/ (10.1126/science.aej2383). Notice fulltext inaccessible; no unverified account of its cause is asserted.
sources.searchOrigin: Conspiracy-dialogue search -> PubMed -> editorial notice cross-link.

sources.title: Large language models can effectively convince people to believe conspiracies
sources.authors: Thomas H. Costello, Kellin Pelrine, Matthew Kowal, Jasper Timm, Antonio A. Arechar, Jean-Francois Godbout, Adam Gleave, David G. Rand and Gordon Pennycook
sources.design: Four experiments varying direction of LLM persuasion, corrections, accuracy constraints and model behavior.
sources.population: 3,996 Americans in the inspected v3 abstract.
sources.geography: United States.
sources.duration: Short experiments; v1 January 8, v3 July 15, 2026; field dates not established.
sources.measure: Conspiracy beliefs, reversal after correction, mock sharing and refusal behavior.
sources.finding: The abstract reports no consistent persuasive advantage for truth over falsehood under permissive instructions. Corrections could reverse induced beliefs, accuracy constraints reduced misinformation persuasion, and GPT-5.2 largely refused pro-conspiracy requests.
sources.limitations: Prompt permissions and guardrails matter; short experimental belief changes and mock sharing are not real-world campaign reach. Preprint and abstract-only extraction.
sources.locator: v3 abstract and version history
sources.sourceNote: Inspected latest author abstract and official title, not full protocols. Earlier v1 counts and framing were not carried forward.
sources.searchOrigin: Costello 2024 citation trail -> 2026 pro-/anti-conspiracy experiments, version check.

sources.title: Reducing belief in conspiracy theories as they unfold using large language models
sources.authors: Thomas H. Costello, Nathaniel Rabb, Michael Nicholas Stagnaro, Gordon Pennycook and David G. Rand
sources.design: Experiments after two real events comparing relevant AI dialogues with irrelevant dialogue or static factual information.
sources.population: US samples of 472 after the July 2024 Trump assassination attempt and 1,042 after the September 2025 Kirk assassination, per v2.
sources.geography: United States.
sources.duration: Immediate effects plus one-to-two-month follow-up; v2 October 19, 2026.
sources.measure: Event-specific conspiracy belief and later beliefs about other conspiracies.
sources.finding: The latest abstract reports immediate reductions. Evidence of downstream protection against other conspiracy beliefs is mixed or suggestive across analyses rather than uniformly durable.
sources.limitations: Event-specific recruitment and attrition details were not inspected. Preprint; no extrapolation to general immunity against misinformation.
sources.locator: v2 abstract and submission history
sources.sourceNote: Official title and v2 abstract inspected at the current arXiv record; version-specific fulltext retrieval failed. Uses v2 sample count, not the earlier 1,035 figure.
sources.searchOrigin: Recent update search -> arXiv August 2026 paper -> October 19 revision.

sources.title: GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers
sources.authors: Weixin Liang, Mert Yuksekgonul, Yining Mao, Eric Wu and James Zou
sources.design: Benchmark of seven detectors on human essays plus model-based editing and generated-text evasion tests.
sources.population: 91 TOEFL essays from a Chinese educational forum and 88 US eighth-grade essays; additional generated essays and abstracts.
sources.geography: English texts; Chinese-source TOEFL corpus and US school corpus.
sources.duration: One benchmark campaign; manuscript v3 July 10, 2023.
sources.measure: False positives by corpus and detection changes after linguistic editing.
sources.finding: Detectors mislabeled non-native English essays much more often in these corpora. Simple rewriting also reduced detection of generated text, showing attribution depends on style as well as provenance.
sources.limitations: Small unmatched corpora differ in task and writer characteristics; old detector versions. Cannot generalize to all languages or all detection methods.
sources.locator: Results: GPT detectors exhibit bias; Simple prompt can easily bypass; Discussion limitations
sources.sourceNote: Full author HTML main results and limitations inspected; no detector rerun. Paired with the Czech replication rather than treating the language effect as universal.
sources.searchOrigin: Synthetic content detection limits -> original Liang paper -> v3 full HTML.

sources.title: Different Time, Different Language: Revisiting the Bias Against Non-Native Speakers in GPT Detectors
sources.authors: Adnan Al Ali, Jindrich Helcl and Jindrich Libovicky
sources.design: Czech corpus comparisons and tests of naive Bayes, RoBERTa and commercial detectors across genres and proficiency groups.
sources.population: 450 native and 450 non-native student essays, smaller advanced-writing samples and additional Czech text corpora.
sources.geography: Czech-language writing.
sources.duration: Single benchmark, v1 February 5, 2026; not a writer follow-up.
sources.measure: Entropy/perplexity patterns, detector false positives and cross-domain behavior.
sources.finding: No systematic non-native penalty emerged across tested Czech conditions, contrasting with the earlier English study. Performance still depended on detector and text domain.
sources.limitations: Language, detector vintage, proficiency and corpus construction all differ from English studies. This is not a direct falsification of the original English result; some recent corpus provenance is uncertain.
sources.locator: Sections 3-5: datasets, entropy and detector comparisons
sources.sourceNote: Full HTML relevant methods/results and official arXiv bibliographic metadata inspected. No detector rerun or raw-data replication.
sources.searchOrigin: Liang replication search -> Czech EACL 2026 author manuscript.

sources.title: Can AI-Generated Text be Reliably Detected?
sources.authors: Vinu Sankar Sadasivan, Aounon Kumar, Sriram Balasubramanian, Wenxiao Wang and Soheil Feizi
sources.publisher: Transactions on Machine Learning Research; arXiv
sources.design: Paraphrasing attacks against detector families and watermarks, supplemented by theoretical indistinguishability analysis.
sources.population: Generated passages and detector benchmarks; approximately 300-token passages described in abstract.
sources.geography: Text benchmark, not a representative human population.
sources.duration: Single research program; v1 March 2023, inspected v4 January 17, 2025.
sources.measure: Detection performance under recursive paraphrase, text quality and spoofing vulnerability.
sources.finding: Repeated paraphrasing can substantially weaken tested detectors, often with limited quality loss; the paper also identifies spoofing risks.
sources.limitations: Attack benchmarks and theoretical conditions do not prove every provenance method is useless. Coverage depends on model, text length, access and threat model.
sources.locator: v4 abstract and version history
sources.sourceNote: Author abstract inspected; attack implementation and full proofs not reviewed.
sources.searchOrigin: Synthetic text detection robustness -> Sadasivan et al., latest version.

sources.title: What AI headline testing reveals about audience engagement
sources.authors: Chartbeat
sources.design: Vendor analysis of publisher headline A/B tests; within-test audience randomization does not randomize publisher adoption of AI.
sources.population: Completed headline tests on participating Chartbeat publisher sites; total test denominator not supplied in inspected article.
sources.geography: Participating publisher network; country mix unspecified.
sources.duration: January-June 2025 tests; exact article publication day not verified.
sources.measure: Click-through lift and win share for AI variants, original headlines and tests with or without AI.
sources.finding: AI variants and original headlines had similar win shares. Tests containing AI variants had larger reported lifts than other tests, but the between-test comparison does not establish a causal adoption effect.
sources.limitations: Selective tool adoption, manual AI labeling, missing total denominator and limited uncertainty reporting. Clicks do not establish comprehension, trust or creator compensation.
sources.locator: Win-rate and CTR-lift sections; study period description
sources.sourceNote: Original vendor article inspected. Repeated comparable headline experiments, not a recurring representative series; no raw experiment analysis.
sources.searchOrigin: AI headline click experiments -> original Chartbeat research article, replacing secondary coverage.

sources.title: Fact-checking information from large language models can decrease headline discernment
sources.authors: Matthew R. DeVerna, Harry Yaojun Yan, Kai-Cheng Yang and Filippo Menczer
sources.publisher: PNAS; PubMed abstract and figure captions
sources.design: Preregistered randomized news-headline judgment experiment comparing LLM and human fact checks, with forced and optional exposure.
sources.population: Online participants evaluating selected news headlines; denominator not extracted from inspected abstract.
sources.geography: Recruitment geography not verified in inspected material.
sources.duration: Short experimental sessions; publication December 10, 2024.
sources.measure: True/false headline discernment and sharing intentions.
sources.finding: LLM checks did not significantly improve overall discernment, whereas human checks did. Wrongly labeling true headlines or expressing uncertainty about false ones could worsen judgments; some correctly labeled items improved sharing intentions.
sources.limitations: Immediate judgments and intentions are not actual sharing. Optional-exposure subgroups are selected, and one model/task cannot establish all AI checking is harmful.
sources.locator: Abstract; Figures 1-3 captions
sources.sourceNote: Primary abstract and captions inspected; fulltext inaccessible. No effect size or unverified sample denominator extracted.
sources.selectionReason: Preregistered comparative design supplies important null and conditional positive evidence, but only abstract-level assessment is available.
sources.headline: AI fact checks did not improve discernment overall in this experiment
sources.searchOrigin: Human-AI belief and fact-check experiment search -> original PNAS abstract.

sources.title: SoA survey reveals a third of translators and quarter of illustrators losing work to AI
sources.authors: Society of Authors
sources.design: Voluntary association survey of members and other authors about AI use, work loss and perceived income effects.
sources.population: Nearly 800 respondents across writing, translation and illustration; occupation-specific denominators not reported in the inspected summary.
sources.geography: UK-centered authors' association; respondent geography not fully established.
sources.duration: January 2024 survey; April 11, 2024 publication with later webpage update.
sources.measure: Self-reported lost commissions and income attributed to AI.
sources.finding: Some responding translators and illustrators reported lost work and falling income attributed to AI. These reports describe affected respondents, not an estimated causal income loss for the whole profession.
sources.limitations: Self-selection, retrospective attribution and missing subgroup denominators; no administrative earnings panel or contemporaneous control group.
sources.locator: Survey findings by profession and survey-method note
sources.sourceNote: Association's original survey summary inspected. A later page update is not a new survey wave; percentage headlines not repeated without subgroup counts.
sources.searchOrigin: Creator income AI translators illustrators -> original Society of Authors survey.

sources.title: Who Is AI Replacing? The Impact of Generative AI on Online Freelancing Platforms
sources.authors: Ozge Demirci, Jonas Hannane and Xinrong Zhu
sources.design: Observational platform job-posting panel comparing more AI-exposed categories with less-exposed work around model releases.
sources.population: Job advertisements on a large online freelance platform; not a panel of creator bank-account earnings.
sources.geography: Online freelance market; country composition not established in abstract.
sources.duration: Includes eight months after ChatGPT release; online publication January 24, 2025, issue October 2025.
sources.measure: Posting volume, remaining-job complexity and offered pay.
sources.finding: The abstract reports a 21% relative decline in writing/coding postings versus manual-intensive categories over eight months after ChatGPT and a 17% decline in image-creation postings after image generators. Remaining jobs were more complex and better paid as advertised.
sources.limitations: Observational category comparisons depend on identification assumptions. Postings and offered pay are not hires, paid hours or realized creator income.
sources.locator: Repository abstract and publication metadata
sources.sourceNote: Institutional author abstract inspected; full regression specifications and robustness checks were not reviewed. Repeated category-level demand observations, not same-worker earnings follow-up.
sources.selectionReason: Direct labor-demand evidence complements creator self-reports; selected as a bounded abstract-level result, not an earnings estimate.
sources.headline: Freelance job demand is measurable, but it is not creator income
sources.searchOrigin: Generative AI creator work empirical study -> Imperial repository for final Management Science article.

sources.title: Generative AI and News Report 2025: How People Think about AI's Role in Journalism and Society
sources.authors: Felix M. Simon, Rasmus Kleis Nielsen and Richard Fletcher
sources.publisher: Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism
sources.design: Online YouGov country surveys compared with a 2024 wave; repeated cross-sections rather than the same respondents followed.
sources.population: Online adult samples in six countries; pooled figures are cross-country averages, not world population estimates.
sources.geography: Argentina, Denmark, France, Japan, UK and US.
sources.duration: June 5-July 15, 2025 fieldwork; report October 7; comparison with 2024.
sources.measure: Self-reported AI use for news, trust, comfort with AI journalism and claimed search-click behavior.
sources.finding: Reported use of AI for news increased from a low base, while preferences for human oversight and concerns about AI journalism persisted.
sources.limitations: Self-reported usage and clicks differ from behavioral logs. Six-country online samples do not represent all regions; wave comparability is not individual change.
sources.locator: Executive summary, methodology and news-use sections
sources.sourceNote: Report webpage relevant sections inspected; underlying survey data not reanalyzed.
sources.searchOrigin: Cross-country AI news audience evidence -> Reuters Institute 2025 report.

sources.title: Algorithmic Effects on the Diversity of Consumption on Spotify
sources.authors: Ashton Anderson, Lucas Maystre, Rishabh Mehrotra, Ian Anderson and Mounia Lalmas
sources.design: Large-scale listening-log analysis plus recommendation experiments; foundational non-generative recommender evidence.
sources.population: Spotify users; paper describes more than 100 million users across several years.
sources.geography: Spotify platform; national composition not extracted.
sources.duration: Several years of logs plus shorter experiments; precise extraction window not verified.
sources.measure: Embedding-based consumption diversity, organic versus algorithmic listening, recommendation relevance and retention.
sources.finding: Algorithmic listening was associated with lower diversity; increasing diversity tended to involve organic listening. Recommendation improvements could benefit listeners differently according to their existing tastes.
sources.limitations: Observational channel-diversity associations are not themselves causal narrowing effects. Music-space embeddings, exposure and consumption are distinct; this is not a generative-AI study.
sources.locator: Abstract, introductory findings and diversity-measure discussion
sources.sourceNote: Author PDF main introductory and measurement passages inspected; not all experiments or appendices. Longitudinal label refers to user listening trajectories, not every component.
sources.searchOrigin: Earlier algorithmic cultural consumption diversity -> author-hosted Spotify study.

sources.title: Experimental Study of Inequality and Unpredictability in an Artificial Cultural Market
sources.authors: Matthew J. Salganik, Peter Sheridan Dodds and Duncan J. Watts
sources.design: Randomized artificial music market with independent choices versus social information and parallel market worlds.
sources.population: 14,341 participants evaluating 48 initially unfamiliar songs; recruitment centered on a youth-oriented website.
sources.geography: Online experiment; not a national representative sample.
sources.duration: One experimental market campaign; individual participation was brief.
sources.measure: Downloads, concentration of success and variation in rankings between parallel worlds.
sources.finding: Social influence increased inequality and unpredictability of song success. Underlying quality mattered but did not fully determine which songs became popular.
sources.limitations: No AI treatment, no actual creator-income estimate and a selected participant pool. Included as a mechanism separating available supply from socially amplified attention.
sources.locator: Main paper experimental design and results
sources.sourceNote: Primary author PDF main paper inspected; supplementary material not fully assessed.
sources.searchOrigin: Foundational cultural-market social influence experiment -> Princeton author paper.

sources.title: On the conversational persuasiveness of GPT-4
sources.authors: Francesco Salvi, Manoel Horta Ribeiro, Riccardo Gallotti and Robert West
sources.publisher: Nature Human Behaviour; Princeton publication record
sources.design: Randomized debates varying human versus GPT-4 opponent, personalization and opinion strength.
sources.population: 900 participants in the final publication abstract.
sources.geography: Participant geography not verified in inspected abstract.
sources.duration: Short debates and immediate opinion measurement; online May 19, 2025, issue August.
sources.measure: Post-debate agreement shift and odds of persuasion in pairwise comparisons.
sources.finding: Personalized GPT-4 was more persuasive than human opponents in the reported comparison; personalization materially changed the result.
sources.limitations: Conditional pairwise success and odds ratios are not percentage-point population belief changes. Short, structured debates do not establish durable influence or campaign-scale effectiveness.
sources.locator: Institutional abstract and publication metadata
sources.sourceNote: Final abstract inspected; publisher fulltext unavailable. Earlier preprint sample of 820 is not mixed with final 900.
sources.searchOrigin: Human versus GPT-4 persuasion -> final Princeton publication record; earlier arXiv version de-duplicated.

sources.title: AI models collapse when trained on recursively generated data
sources.authors: Ilia Shumailov, Zakhar Shumaylov, Yiren Zhao, Nicolas Papernot, Ross Anderson and Yarin Gal
sources.design: Computational experiments and mathematical analysis of recursive synthetic training-data replacement.
sources.population: Model-generated training distributions, not observed cultural populations.
sources.geography: Not geographically defined.
sources.duration: Successive training generations in controlled experiments; published 2024, author correction linked March 21, 2025.
sources.measure: Distribution-tail retention and model degradation across training generations.
sources.finding: Recursive replacement with synthetic data can erase distribution tails and degrade tested models.
sources.limitations: Not evidence that all synthetic-data use collapses, that culture is already collapsing, or that the Internet contains a particular synthetic share. Data retention and training setup matter.
sources.locator: Abstract, recursive-training results and correction link
sources.sourceNote: Primary article relevant text inspected. Linked 2025 correction could not be inspected, so no detailed quantitative claims or core selection. Repeated means computational generations, not human follow-up.
sources.searchOrigin: Cultural diversity synthetic training feedback -> Nature original and correction metadata.

sources.title: Is Model Collapse Inevitable? Breaking the Curse of Recursion by Accumulating Real and Synthetic Data
sources.authors: Matthias Gerstgrasser et al.
sources.design: Model-training experiments and theoretical analysis contrasting data replacement with accumulation retaining real data.
sources.population: Computational training distributions and tested model architectures.
sources.geography: Not geographically defined.
sources.duration: Successive training generations; v2 April 29, 2024.
sources.measure: Model performance under different recursive data-management regimes.
sources.finding: Retaining real data and accumulating rather than replacing training data avoided collapse under the tested conditions.
sources.limitations: Conditional technical counterexample, not measured cultural diversity or a guarantee for every future training regime.
sources.locator: v2 abstract and version history
sources.sourceNote: Author abstract inspected; experimental details and proof assumptions not fully reviewed.
sources.searchOrigin: Model collapse counterevidence -> real/synthetic accumulation study.

sources.title: Generative artificial intelligence, human creativity, and art
sources.authors: Eric Zhou and Dokyun Lee
sources.design: Observational artist-platform panel comparing adoption and changes over time, with never-/not-yet-treated comparisons.
sources.population: More than 4 million artworks from more than 50,000 users.
sources.geography: Online art platform; geographic composition not established in inspected material.
sources.duration: Monthly user outcomes before and after adoption; precise dates not verified; publication March 5, 2024.
sources.measure: Posting productivity, favorites per view, average/maximum content novelty, visual novelty and concentration of favorites.
sources.finding: The study reports increased productivity and favorites per view, declining average content novelty but increasing maximum content novelty, and declining visual novelty. Favorites became less concentrated among adopters.
sources.limitations: Adoption is not randomized; provenance and platform-selection assumptions need fulltext review. Favorites are engagement, not financial income, and maximum novelty is not average diversity.
sources.locator: Abstract; Figures 1 and 4 captions
sources.sourceNote: Primary abstract and captions inspected; publisher and PMC fulltext retrieval failed. Numerical causal estimates not adopted without methods review.
sources.searchOrigin: Generative AI art diversity positive and negative evidence -> final PNAS Nexus abstract.

sources.title: Co-Writing with Opinionated Language Models Affects Users' Views
sources.authors: Maurice Jakesch, Advait Bhat, Daniel Buschek, Lior Zalmanson and Mor Naaman
sources.design: Controlled co-writing experiment with language-model assistance biased toward opposing views about social media.
sources.population: 1,506 writers and 500 independent judges reported in abstract.
sources.geography: Online recruitment; geography not verified in abstract.
sources.duration: Single writing task and immediate post-task measurement; v1 February 1, 2023.
sources.measure: Position expressed in writing and participants' subsequent stated attitudes.
sources.finding: Opinionated assistance shifted both written arguments and immediate reported views toward the model's position.
sources.limitations: One topic and short exposure; no verified persistence, downstream behavior or evidence of intentional covert manipulation in deployed products.
sources.locator: Abstract and bibliographic metadata
sources.sourceNote: Author abstract inspected; prompts, exclusions and full statistical analysis not assessed.
sources.searchOrigin: Human-AI content beliefs writing-assistant experiment -> CHI author manuscript.

gaps.title: Link supply to genuine attention and realized creator income
gaps.summary: These sources measure different stages of a cultural market without a common denominator or linked observation window.
gaps.basis: Deezer separates uploads from listening and fraud; Pew measures search clicks; Chartbeat measures headline experiments; Society of Authors measures attributed income loss; Demirci measures postings and offered pay. Neither engagement gains nor fewer postings identify the same creators' net income.
gaps.next: Build consented creator/platform panels linking provenance, impressions, verified human consumption, payments, commissions and costs. Report fraud filters, rank changes, creator entry/exit and country-specific denominators.

gaps.title: Test durable influence under varied motives and real use
gaps.summary: Short tasks show influence, but its persistence, reach and direction outside experiments remain unevenly established here.
gaps.basis: Salvi and Jakesch show immediate persuasion; DeVerna finds no overall discernment gain and conditional harms/benefits. Recent conspiracy studies vary by prompting and downstream analysis; the 2024 Science result has an editorial concern. These are not interchangeable estimates of societal belief change.
gaps.next: Preregister multi-month naturalistic trials separating exposure, accurate versus inaccurate persuasion, model guardrails, belief, behavior and correction. Include attrition analyses and independent replication.

gaps.title: Measure diversity at multiple levels and over creator careers
gaps.summary: Individual quality, maximum novelty, typical novelty and consumed diversity can point in different directions.
gaps.basis: Doshi finds better-rated but more similar stories; Zhou finds diverging average and peak novelty. Spotify and the cultural-market experiment show selection and social amplification mechanisms, while model-collapse studies concern training distributions rather than human culture.
gaps.next: Follow creators and audiences across languages and genres, combining blinded human judgments with validated similarity measures, exposure logs and retention of minority styles. Separate production, recommendation and consumption pathways.

gaps.title: Validate provenance without universal detector assumptions
gaps.summary: A stable multilingual ground truth for mixed human-AI content is not supplied by this corpus.
gaps.basis: English detector disparities do not recur uniformly in the Czech study; paraphrasing changes detectability. Deezer's proprietary classification and the three-song Ipsos task address different modalities and error units.
gaps.next: Create versioned, consented multilingual and multimodal benchmarks with known editing histories. Measure false positives and negatives by proficiency, genre, model and hybrid workflow, and audit operational prevalence estimates against them.

reviewNotes: Findings apply to the tasks, platforms and populations described, not to all culture. Evidence outside English-language and relatively affluent online settings is limited in this selected corpus.
Inspection depth varies: fulltext status means relevant sections were read, not every supplement or raw dataset; abstract and official-summary records have narrower assessment limits.

The 2024 conspiracy-dialogue article has a June 2026 editorial expression of concern. Its effect should not anchor a confident conclusion while that uncertainty remains; the notice is not a retraction.
The Nature model-collapse article has a linked 2025 correction whose contents were not assessed. Deezer's July 2026 release contains inconsistent tagging-start dates.
Failure to classify all three songs is not a per-song error rate. Peak daily uploads are not catalog share; headline clicks, favorites and advertised pay are not realized creator income.
Repeated surveys, platform disclosures and computational training generations are different from following the same people. Technical model-collapse results do not measure human cultural change.
